transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The government will release its new estimate on the broadest measure of the U.S. economy today,
the gross domestic product.
NPR's Stephen Bisaha says the last quarter report on the GDP showed economic growth.
But there is worry.
This economic growth does feel delicate.
That's according to Mark Zandy, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.
We're growing.
The economy is moving forward, but it's a very, very fragile growth.
It doesn't feel like we're kicking in on all cylinders.
He blames that fragility on inflation and ties it to the Trump administration's policies,
like tariffs in the U.S. war against Iran, which has driven up energy prices.
NPR's Stephen Bisaha reporting.
Separately, we'll get another reading on inflation for the month of September.
Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, Mary Peltola, is dismissing a New York Times report.
It alleges her campaign was part of efforts to put another Senate candidate on the ballot
with the same name as Alaska's incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan.
That recruit is retired teacher, Dan J. Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan, not the incumbent senator, denies this.
Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports Mary Peltola did not directly refute the Times report.
Republicans have alleged for months that the second Sullivan is a Democratic plant
intended to draw votes away from the senator.
The Times story seems to substantiate that claim,
although NPR has not independently confirmed that reporting.
Peltola dismissed the story as a distraction.
Nobody at the New York Times cares about affordability in Alaska.
Super PACs often promote spoilers in Alaska elections.
The state's ranked choice voting method is intended to blunt the spoiler effect.
But not all voters rank their ballots.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
In Israel, more than 90 percent of votes have been counted in Tuesday's election.
No side has secured a majority.
NPR's Daniel Esther reports on what options the candidates may face to break the impasse.
Analysts say Gadi Isinkot, leading the opposition,
may face pressure to enter a unity government with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
During the campaign, Isinkot vowed not to join a Netanyahu-led government.
But Netanyahu has been campaigning to resume the war with Iran.
And if he does, he could take advantage of the crisis to convince Isinkot
to put aside political differences and share power.
Dani Citrinovich is a former Israeli military intelligence officer specializing in Iran.
Netanyahu definitely has an incentive to go to war.
He understands that returning to war against Iran while forming a government will serve his interest.
Isinkot's allies are expected to work fast to replace the Speaker of Parliament to gain political leverage.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
This is NPR.
Spanish officials say that at least 68 people were killed in yesterday's collision of two trains.
They're still investigating the crash seen in central Spain.
The Trump administration will allow compounding pharmacies to make six popular peptides that were previously banned.
NPR's Sydney Luftgen reports the policy change could make the products touted for wellness more widely available.
The Department of Health and Human Services said in a new policy that it will use its enforcement discretion to allow production of the peptides by compounding pharmacies.
That means regulators will look the other way, even though the peptides haven't been rigorously tested or approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to the six peptides through compounding pharmacies.
However, at the same meeting, FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
HHS says the new policy is a safer alternative to the illicit research-use-only peptides that consumers use now.
Sydney Luftgen, NPR News.
The Federal Trade Commission is telling several big companies to hand over data that show how they set prices for customers.
The FTC issued this demand to Walmart, Delta Airlines and DoorDash, among other firms.
The agency says that it wants to look at whether these companies set prices based on factors such as the analysis of personal data or whether consumers belong to the company's loyalty programs.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Government to release new GDP estimate; economist Mark Zandy calls growth fragile
Inflation reading for September due out; blamed on tariffs and Iran war energy prices
Mary Peltola dismisses New York Times report on campaign recruiting same-name Senate candidate
Israel's election vote count passes 90 percent; no side secures a majority
Netanyahu may pressure opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot into unity government over Iran war
Spain says at least 68 killed in collision of two trains in central Spain
HHS to let compounding pharmacies make six previously banned peptides
FTC orders Walmart, Delta, DoorDash to hand over data on how they set prices
